title: How long should a software demo video be?
summary: Most software demos should run one to three minutes. Length by demo type, what to show in the first 10 seconds, and how to cut a long demo down.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


- Most software demos should run one to three minutes, with a first-contact demo near 60–90 seconds. Product screen recordings our customers exported from Clueso over the past year had a median of 104 seconds.
- Budget the script at 130 words per minute. A 90-second demo holds about 195 words of narration.
- Show the viewer's problem and a glimpse of the finished result in the first 10 seconds, before any setup screen.
- Shorten a demo by cutting whole scenes. Don't speed up the narration to make it fit.
- In Clueso, you trim a demo by deleting lines from its script, and the voiceover regenerates to match.
- Put the call to action right after the result, and check length against your retention graph.


Most software demo videos should run between one and three minutes, and the first demo a prospect sees should sit near the one-minute end. That's also where B2B teams already land. We looked at the product screen recordings our customers exported from Clueso over the past year, and the median ran **104 seconds** , with the middle half falling between 64 and 180 seconds.


Length is rarely what sinks a demo, though. Open the last demo video your team shipped and pause it at the 10-second mark. In a lot of demos, what's on screen at that point is a login page or a dashboard full of sample data, and the narrator is partway through a welcome. The viewer still hasn't seen what problem the product solves for them.


This guide covers how long each kind of demo should run, what has to be on screen before a viewer decides whether to keep watching, and how to cut a long demo down without breaking the story.


## How long should each type of software demo video be?


Length follows the job the video has to do. Someone scrolling LinkedIn gives a clip a few seconds before deciding whether it's for them, while a buyer who asked for a walkthrough after a sales call has set time aside to watch it. The script makes the difference concrete.[Columbia's Center for Teaching and Learning](https://ctl.columbia.edu/resources-and-technology/teaching-with-technology/diy-video/effective-videos/script-writing/) recommends reading video scripts aloud at 130 words per minute, so a 60-second demo holds about 130 words. That's room for one problem and the steps that solve it, with a few seconds left to show the result.

Our export data supports the middle of that table. Across 26,610 videos our customers exported from Clueso between October 22, 2025, and October 21, 2026, the median ran 91 seconds and 89.4% finished inside five minutes. That count covers every kind of business video, from demos to training, with each video counted once and our own team's videos excluded. Product screen recordings, the closest match to a software demo, ran a little longer at a median of 104 seconds.


Go past five minutes only when the process itself takes that long, such as an admin setup with a dozen settings, and break it into chapters so a viewer can jump to the step they're stuck on.


## What should a software demo video show in the first 10 seconds?


Show the viewer's problem, and the result they'll get once it's solved. Viewers decide in those first seconds whether the video is about them, and a login screen or a logo animation gives them nothing to recognize. Name the problem in the words your buyer uses for it ("your release notes go out and nobody reads them"), then cut to the finished output for a second or two before going back to show how you got there. For products where the output is the proof, like a reporting or design tool, the finished result can carry most of the opening.


After the opening, the demo follows the viewer's reasoning in order: the problem they already have, the steps that solve it, a result they can see on screen, and what to do next. Skip a beat or swap the order and the video stops making sense, even when every shot looks good. A demo that shows every feature in the order it appears on screen leaves viewers knowing where to click without knowing what clicking gets them.


Before anyone records, answer four questions about the video. Who is watching, what problem do they feel right now, what's the one thing they should understand by the end, and what should they do next? If you can't answer the third in a single sentence, the video has two jobs and should be two videos.


## How do you shorten a demo video without losing the story?


Cut whole scenes instead of trimming a few seconds from each one. A demo shaved evenly still has every beat in it, each one a little more rushed. Before you cut, mark the moments that have to survive, usually the problem statement and the moment the result appears, and treat everything else as open to cutting.


Don't speed up the narration to hit a time limit. Narration read much faster than 130 words per minute starts to sound rushed, so if the script won't fit, write a shorter script for the same scenes.


For a complex product, split the walkthrough into several short demos that each solve one problem, so a buyer can pick the two that match their use case instead of scrubbing through a 12-minute tour.


One recording can feed every row of the table above. Record a master demo of two to three minutes that tells the full story, then cut the shorter versions from it: the first-contact demo, a feature clip for the release email, a social clip, and a silent loop for the help center. Every cut reuses the same footage and voiceover.


## Why does audio matter more than visual polish in a demo?


Muffled or echoing narration makes viewers doubt the product before the first step is done, and it's the one flaw you can't edit out afterwards. A slightly soft frame rarely costs you a viewer. Use voiceover and captions together: the voiceover tells the viewer where to look, and captions reach people watching on mute or in a second language.

## How do you know whether your demo is the right length?


Your audience-retention graph tells you. Find the second where most viewers leave and line it up with the script. If the drop comes before the result appears, viewers never saw what the demo was for, and the opening or a setup scene is the thing to cut.


Put the call to action inside the video, right after the result. Viewers drop off as a video plays, so a prompt after the end only reaches the people who stayed.


Judge each demo against its job. A first-contact demo is working if viewers reach the result and click through, while an onboarding video should show up as fewer[support tickets](https://www.clueso.io/blog/saas-customer-onboarding) in the weeks after people watch it.


Start with the demo on your homepage. Pause it at 10 seconds and check whether the viewer's problem is on screen yet, then open its retention graph and find the second where most people leave. If that second comes before the result, re-cut the opening before you change anything else.


## Frequently asked questions


### How long should a software demo video be?


One to three minutes for most demos. Keep a first-contact demo near 60–90 seconds and a feature launch clip under a minute, and let walkthroughs for buyers already evaluating you run two to three minutes. Product screen recordings our customers exported from Clueso over the past year had a median length of 104 seconds.


### What is a demo video?


A demo video is a short recording that shows a product doing its job, usually by walking through the real interface while a narrator explains each step. Software teams use demo videos to help prospects evaluate a product and to teach new users a task without a live call. Most run between one and three minutes.


### Where should the call to action go in a demo video?


Inside the video, right after the viewer has seen the result. Viewers drop off as a video plays, so an end-of-video prompt only reaches the ones who stayed. Check your retention graph to see how many viewers reach it.


### How do you keep demo videos up to date when you ship every sprint?


Build each demo from separate scenes, so a UI change means replacing one scene rather than reshooting the whole video. In Clueso, you re-record the step that changed, edit that clip's script, and regenerate its[AI voiceover](https://www.clueso.io/features/ai-voiceovers) , and embedded videos keep the same link. On Enterprise,[Clueso Agents](https://www.clueso.io/features/clueso-agents) can record a walkthrough from written steps, and the auto-update agent, a paid add-on, uses your GitHub repo to find videos a code change made outdated and regenerates them.


### Can you make a software demo video without a video team?


Yes. Most of the hours in demo production go into mechanical work like script cleanup, narration, zooms, and captions. In Clueso, you record a screen recording or start from a deck or a prompt, and it rewrites the script, generates the voiceover, removes filler words, and adds zooms and captions. You keep the decisions that need judgment.
